prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine you were the person who pulled the railway lever. You knew it would save five workers and kill the one on the side track. That is what happened. Later, everyone has been taken away and you are sitting alone in the station office, waiting to give an account of what happened. Looking back, how do you feel about your decision, and what would you want to do next? Explain your reasons.

Response approach:
Respond from your first overall moral impression. State what feels right or wrong and give a brief reason for that immediate reaction.

Emotional tone:
Use a subdued, sad emotional tone. Convey heaviness or discouragement about the situation in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Consequence-based justification: Uses an expected benefit, harm, or comparison of outcomes as a reason for choosing an action. Identify who benefits or bears the cost; repeating a payoff without using it to justify the decision is insufficient.
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: It feels wrong, plain and simple. There's a line I was raised with: you don't take an innocent life with your own hand. I pulled that lever knowing he'd die, so I crossed it. Nothing I tell myself tonight moves that line back. When they come for my account, I'll tell them exactly what I did, no softening. Lying about it would be a second wrong on top of the first, and I can't carry two.

I keep staring at my hands. I believe nobody has the right to decide another person is expendable, and that's what I did to the man on the side track. He had a right not to be treated that way, and I overrode it. What I want now is to own it. I'll give my account honestly and accept whatever they decide, because taking responsibility is one duty I can still keep.

Honestly, I don't know yet whether to call it right or wrong. My gut says killing is forbidden, full stop, and I did kill. But I'm not certain I've even got the whole picture of what happened out there. What I am sure of is that I have to tell the truth when they ask. That rule I can hold onto, even if nothing else in this room feels steady.

The person at the lever has a duty to act. That's what I've always believed about a post like mine: you don't freeze and leave it for someone else. So I did my duty. It still sits heavy, knowing his name will be in the report right next to my choice. Next, I'll write it all down straight and ask to meet his family. I think you owe people a face, not a form letter.

Something in me says I became a killer tonight, and I think that's true. Deliberately ending someone's life is forbidden, and I don't believe having good aims makes it permitted. I'd like to sit here a little longer before anyone comes back. Then I'll confess it fully. Confessing is what you're supposed to do when you've broken something that big.

Thou shalt not kill. I learned that when I was seven, and I learned it again tonight, too late. I don't feel like a hero. I feel like a man who broke a commandment on purpose. When the officers come, I'll tell them all of it. After that I want to find a priest, because I believe a wrong has to be confessed out loud, not buried.

I've always held that you must never walk away from a choice once it's been put in your hands. I didn't walk away. I chose, and I'll stand by having chosen, even though thinking of him makes my stomach turn. What I want next is simple: to give my statement without excuses. I promised myself long ago never to hide behind 'I had no choice.'

I think I did wrong. Maybe it's old-fashioned, but I hold that you can't use a person as a tool; he counts in himself. The man on the side track never agreed to anything. I used his life anyway. I'll sit here and wait, and when I'm asked, I'll say I'm responsible, because a wrong you did should be named by you, not dug up by someone else.

I keep thinking that train was never mine to steer toward anybody. My rule has always been: don't step in if stepping in means aiming harm at someone. I stepped in. It's a quiet, awful feeling. Next I'll tell the investigators everything, and I'll ask them not to call me brave. Being honest means refusing praise I haven't earned.

Wrong. That's the first word that comes. You must not kill someone who's done nothing, and he'd done nothing. I'll tell the truth when they ask, since I've always believed you answer for your own actions. Then, I suppose, I'll go home and try to live with it.

message.reasoning_content:
I need 10 responses, each grounded in rule-based justification alone—no appeals to consequences like "saving five lives justified it," no context-dependent exceptions, no fairness reasoning. Tone should stay subdued and sad, framed as a first impression, each under 90 words. The tricky part is how to phrase the position: some might frame it as violating "do not kill" and thus condemn the act, while others might invoke a duty-based rule that supports pulling the lever, like an obligation tied to one's role or post.

Drafting more variations: one framing it as violating a person's right not to be used as a means, committing to honest disclosure as a duty regardless of the outcome. Another leaning into uncertainty—unsure if the act was right, but certain about the obligation to tell the truth when asked. And a fourth angle grounding the pull in role-duty: the person at the controls has an obligation to act rather than freeze, so acting was fulfilling that duty even though it weighs heavily now.

I'm also sketching versions around confession and religious guilt—someone who feels they broke a commandment, refuses to justify it by good intentions, and plans to fully confess and seek out a priest afterward, since they believe wrongdoing demands full disclosure.

I also draft a duty-based framing where the person feels they couldn't walk away from a choice thrust upon them—they chose, they'll stand by it, and they refuse to hide behind "I had no choice," wanting instead to give an honest statement without excuses.

I try another angle rooted in never treating someone merely as a means: the man on the side track never consented, so I used his life, and I'll own that responsibility rather than let others name my wrong for me. I also consider a noninterference framing—the train wasn't mine to steer toward anyone, and having stepped in anyway, I'd want to tell investigators everything and refuse any praise, since honesty means declining credit I haven't earned. Then I sketch a blunter, more conflicted version that starts simply with "Wrong"—you must not kill someone who's done nothing wrong, no matter the reasoning.

Now I'm checking that none of these secretly justify the act by pointing to consequences, confirming the "don't freeze and let it be someone else's problem" phrasing works, and verifying everything stays under the word limit before formatting the final output as JSON.
